name: Anti-fascism
summary: Anti-fascism is opposition to fascism drawn from many political traditions: communist, socialist, anarchist, liberal, Christian conservative, monarchist and nationalist. Its defining scholarship reduces it to a minimum: fundamental hostility to fascism, grounded in Enlightenment values such as equality, liberty, progress, toleration and universality, including rejection of fascism's racial inequality, ultra-nationalism and expansionism. Beyond that core its strands disagree, for example on democracy against one-party rule, on revolution, and on violence.
scope: Anti-fascism as a family of opposition to fascism from the 1920s to today, answered only from comparative scholarship that defines it: Nigel Copsey's 'anti-fascist minimum' (his Afterword to Anti-Fascism in European History, 2023), the introduction to that volume by Pirjevec, Pelikan and Ramet, the introduction to Rethinking Antifascism by García, Yusta, Tabet and Clímaco (2016), Enzo Traverso's essay on intellectuals and anti-fascism, and Jens Späth's Docupedia-Zeitgeschichte entry (2019). Member movements' own texts (Comintern resolutions, the Popular Front, resistance programmes, the Italian constitution) and the record of states that used anti-fascism as a legitimating ideology (the GDR, Socialist Yugoslavia, whose doctrine was Marxism-Leninism) do not answer for it; the modern militant antifa movement has its own entry. Where the defining sources document division among anti-fascists the answer is 0 low.

notes: Anti-fascism is answered as a family: its defining scholarship (Copsey, Pirjevec/Pelikan/Ramet, García et al., Traverso, Späth, Rabinbach) defines it as hostility to fascism grounded in Enlightenment values and stresses that its strands (communist, socialist, anarchist, liberal, Christian conservative, monarchist, nationalist) disagree on most else; Ramet et al. call it 'not a consistent ideology' and Copsey 'no ideology, thick or thin'. So only positions the definition itself settles (racial inequality, expansionism, war, national rebirth, progress) are answered, and documented divisions (democracy versus one-party rule, revolution, violence, totalitarianism) are 0 low. Member movements' texts and the record of states that used anti-fascism to legitimate communist rule (GDR, Yugoslavia) are not used. Themes searched after the uncertainty check: world and globalism (international organisations, sovereignty, foreign alliances; the sources mention a cosmopolitan, transnational activism but no position on institutions), gender and family (women's anti-fascism and feminism appear as strands, with no family-wide position), minorities and self-determination (the Slovene and South Tyrol cases are member movements), economy (Comintern anti-capitalism versus non-Marxist anti-fascism, no common position).
